Pennyworth
pen'ny-wurth
n. (as much as a penny will buy; the value of a penny)
From penny and worth. In the Authorized Version penny renders the Greek denarion, a Roman coin worth a labourer's day wage — so two hundred pennyworth is most of a year's work.

Biblical Definition

Both occurrences record the disciples doing arithmetic in front of the Bread of Life. Mark: “He answered and said unto them, Give ye them to eat. And they say unto him, Shall we go and buy two hundred pennyworth of bread, and give them to eat?” (Mar 6:37). John gives the same sum to Philip: “Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little” (Joh 6:7). The figure is not rhetorical. A penny was a day's wage for a labourer, so two hundred pennyworth is roughly eight months' earnings, and Philip's point is that even that sum would only yield a little apiece. He is not being faithless in the arithmetic; he is being accurate. His error is that he was asked a question by Someone for whom the calculation was irrelevant — John notes that Christ said it to prove him, for He Himself knew what He would do. Then Andrew produces the real inventory: “There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?” (Joh 6:9). The account closes with twelve baskets over. Between the pennyworth and the baskets lies the whole distance between resources and the Lord of them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines pennyworth as as much as is bought for a penny; and hence any small quantity, or a good bargain.

expand to see more

PEN'NYWORTH, n.

1. As much as is bought for a penny.

2. Any purchase; any thing bought or sold for money.

3. A good bargain; as, to buy a thing at a pennyworth.

4. A small quantity. Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them. John 6. The penny of the Authorized Version is the Roman denarius, a day's wages for a labourer.

Key Scripture

Mark 6:37 — "He answered and said unto them, Give ye them to eat. And they say unto him, Shall we go and buy two hundred pennyworth of bread, and give them to eat?"

John 6:7 — "Philip answered him, Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little."

John 6:9 — "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?"

Matthew 6:3 — "But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth:"

Modern Corruption

The feeding is reduced to a parable about sharing, which turns a miracle of creation into a lesson in generosity and loses the point of the arithmetic.

expand to see more

The favourite liberal rendering of the feeding of the five thousand is that the crowd had food hidden in their cloaks and Christ's example moved them to share it — the real miracle being one of generosity. The pennyworth is what defeats that reading. John records the exact sum because the Evangelist wants the reader to know that the resources were counted, found insufficient by a wide margin, and that the counting was invited by Christ specifically to prove Philip. A story about shared lunches would not need the audit, and it would not need the twelve baskets of surplus at the end. The apostolic church preached a Christ who creates bread, which is why John builds the whole discourse on the bread of life out of it.

There is a practical corruption for churches too, and it is the Philip habit. Confronted with a work God has plainly commanded, the first instinct is to total the resources, compare them to the need, and conclude the thing cannot be done — and the arithmetic is usually correct. Philip was right about the money. Andrew was closer, because he at least brought the five loaves to Christ while admitting what they were worth. The dictionary's counsel is not to despise the accounting; stewardship requires it. It is to remember Whose hands the accounts are put into afterwards.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek denarion (G1220), the Roman denarius, a day's wage; diakosion denarion, two hundred pence; artos (G740), bread, a loaf.

expand to see more

Greek denarion (G1220) — the Roman denarius; Matthew 20:2 fixes it as a day's wage for a labourer in the vineyard.

Greek diakosion denarion artoi (G1250, G1220) — two hundred denarii of loaves; Mark 6:37 and John 6:7, some eight months' wages.

Greek peirazon auton (G3985) — proving him; John 6:6, the question was a test with the answer already settled.

Greek brachu ti (G1024) — a little something; Philip's estimate of each man's portion even at that price.

Greek kophinous (G2894) — the twelve wicker baskets of fragments that closed the account.

Usage

"“Two hundred pennyworth of bread” — eight months of a labourer's wages, and Philip was right."

"“What are they among so many?” — Andrew brought them anyway."

"“That every one of them may take a little” — accurate arithmetic, wrong question."
